content: Greater celandine, scientifically known as Chelidonium majus and also referred to as tetterwort, is a yellow-flowering plant belonging to the poppy family. It is native to Europe and the Mediterranean region but has become widespread in North America, where it was introduced by settlers as early as 1672 for its use as an herbal remedy for skin conditions such as warts. The plant typically grows to a height of 30 to 120 cm and features an erect stem. Its leaves are deeply divided and can reach up to 30 cm in length. The flowers consist of four yellow petals, each approximately 1 cm long, accompanied by two sepals. These flowers bloom from May to July. The seeds are small, black, and possess an elaiosome, a structure that attracts ants for seed dispersal through a process known as myrmecochory. A naturally occurring double-flowered variety of the plant also exists. However, greater celandine is considered an aggressive invasive species in natural areas such as woods and fields. Control methods primarily involve pulling or spraying the plant before it disperses its seeds. Greater celandine is the sole species within the genus Chelidonium and is not closely related to lesser celandine, which belongs to a different plant family. Pharmacology The entire plant is toxic in moderate doses due to its content of isoquinoline alkaloids. However, when used at appropriate dosages, it has numerous therapeutic applications. The primary alkaloid found in the herb and root is coptisine, while other alkaloids include berberine, chelidonine, sanguinarine, and chelerythrine. Among these, sanguinarine is particularly toxic, with a lethal dose of only 18 mg per kg of body weight. Despite its acute toxicity, sanguinarine is present in such small quantities in the plant that a lethal dose would require the ingestion of over 50 grams of raw herb. The plant also contains caffeic acid derivatives. The fresh herb exhibits mild analgesic, cholagogic (bile-stimulating), antimicrobial, oncostatic (anti-tumor), and central nervous system sedative effects. Animal studies have demonstrated that greater celandine has cytostatic properties and may stimulate the immune system. Some studies suggest that alkaloid extractions from the plant can produce similar effects. The alkaloids are known to cause immobilization in mice when administered orally or via injection. In rabbits, these alkaloids reduce the tone of smooth muscle, causing limpness. Additionally, they have been observed to stimulate the heart and lungs in frogs, cats, and dogs, leading to increased blood pressure and arterial dilation. Early studies on greater celandine revealed that contact with its red-to-yellow latex can cause contact dermatitis and eye irritation. However, these effects have not been observed in animal studies, as no inflammation was noted in rabbit eye tests. The latex can leave a non-permanent stain on the skin, particularly on the fingers, which may sometimes lead to eye irritation if the eyes are rubbed or contact lenses are handled after exposure. If any part of the plant causes eye irritation, it is recommended to rinse the eyes with clear water and seek medical attention if necessary. The latex is also known to stain clothing. Herbalism The aerial parts and roots of greater celandine are used in herbal medicine. The above-ground parts are harvested during the flowering season and dried at high temperatures, while the roots are collected in autumn (between August and October) and dried. The fresh rhizome is also utilized. The plant has a hot and bitter taste, and its latex emits a narcotic fragrance. Preparations are made using alcoholic and hot aqueous extractions, such as teas. The average daily dosage is 2 to 4 grams, equivalent to 12 to 13 mg of total alkaloids. For fluid extracts, the daily dosage is 1 to 2 ml of a 1:1 25% alcoholic extraction, taken up to three times per day. Alternatively, five dessert spoonfuls of the herb steeped in boiling water for 10 minutes can be consumed three times daily. Historically, gypsies used greater celandine as a foot refresher, while modern herbalists value its purgative properties. The plant acts as a mild sedative and has been historically employed to treat asthma, bronchitis, and whooping cough. Its antispasmodic effects improve bile flow in the gallbladder and have been reputed to treat gallstones and gallbladder pain. Dating back to the writings of Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides in the 1st century AD, greater celandine has been recognized as a valuable detoxifying agent. Additionally, the root has been chewed to alleviate toothache.
